description: We are CSE students at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology. Passionate about web development, AI/ML, and UI/UX design, we love transforming complex ideas into intuitive, practical software solutions. As a team, we are driven to solve NASA challenges by blending technology, data visualization, and creative problem-solving.

Users can select a sky region, retrieve archived images, create chronological sky movies, and compare observations to investigate changes. An optional machine-learning model trained on real SPHEREx observations of known asteroids ranks candidate tracks for closer examination, while educational simulations explain orbital motion, the Solar System, and the hypothetical Planet X.

details:
AegisEarth, developed by InfraQ Stargazers, is an interactive astronomy platform designed to help students, educators, and citizen scientists explore NASA’s SPHEREx observations. It addresses the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge by turning archived astronomical images into an accessible experience for investigating the changing sky.

Users enter sky coordinates, select a field of view and observation dates, and retrieve available observations from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). The platform arranges images chronologically to create sky movies, allowing users to inspect the same region over time. Image comparison and difference tools help highlight changes, while observation metadata and archive links provide the context needed to investigate them.

An optional machine-learning component ranks known-object candidate tracks for closer examination. It uses an ensemble of 50 logistic-regression models trained on features extracted from real SPHEREx observations of known asteroids. Candidate ranking supports investigation; it does not independently confirm an unknown object or the existence of Planet X. Interactive educational pages complement the data viewer by explaining SPHEREx, orbital motion, the Solar System, and the hypothetical Planet X.

The project combines React and TypeScript for the web interface with Python and scikit-learn for machine-learning development. Its scientific workflow uses SPHEREx FITS data, IRSA archive services, SkyBoT for known-object candidates, and JPL Horizons positions for preparing training examples.

AegisEarth’s creativity lies in combining real astronomical observations, chronological visualization, machine-learning assistance, and interactive learning within one platform. This connects scientific concepts with hands-on exploration and helps users move from viewing an image to asking questions about the evidence.

The intended impact is to make public space data more approachable, encourage participation in astronomy, and help users identify observations worth further study. During development, our team considered usability, scientific accuracy, data availability, source transparency, and the limits of automated analysis. We also considered how wavelength differences, noise, calibration, and image processing can affect comparisons. These factors shaped a platform that encourages curiosity while helping users interpret results responsibly.
